Where it began

David Lloyd was born in Accrington, Lancashire, on 18 March 1947, and went to Accrington Secondary Technical School. He learned his cricket in the Lancashire League, playing for Accrington from 1962. He was handy at football too, turning out for Accrington Stanley, the club he supported all his life.

His first match for Lancashire, against Middlesex at Old Trafford in June 1965, began with a pair: out without scoring in both innings. He did take two wickets, which was something to tell people about instead. It took until 1968, and an unbeaten 148 against Cambridge University, for the first hundred to arrive.

The player

Lloyd was a left-handed batter and a left-arm spinner, and a proper all-rounder at county level. He played 407 first-class matches, passed 1,000 runs in a season ten times and won three Gillette Cup finals in a row, in 1970, 1971 and 1972. He captained Lancashire from 1973 to 1977.

For England he played nine Tests in 1974 and 1975, scoring 552 runs at 42.46 and holding 11 catches. In only his second Test, against India at Edgbaston in July 1974, he batted for 448 minutes and finished on 214 not out. That winter in Australia an injury cut short his tour, and with it his Test career.

What made him special

He loved the game and never really left it. He became a first-class umpire, standing in 35 first-class matches, then coached Lancashire from 1993 and England from 1996 to the 1999 World Cup. Under him England won Test series against India, New Zealand and South Africa, the last of them their first five-match series win since 1986–87.

If there was a gap in his game, it showed against the fast bowling of Lillee and Thomson that winter in Australia, where his four Tests brought far fewer runs than his summer at home. And in nine Tests his left-arm spin never did produce a wicket.

Away from the middle

To the cricket world he was Bumble, a nickname that came from a likeness to the Bumblies, characters in Michael Bentine's television shows for young viewers. He commentated on Test Match Special and then for Sky Sports from 1999 to 2021, and from 2003 he became the voice of Twenty20 cricket, full of fizz and catchphrases. He liked to slip lines from Half Man Half Biscuit songs into his commentary, and his colleagues often had no idea.

His books included Start the Car and Last in the Tin Bath. His son Graham played six one-day internationals for England. Accrington gave Lloyd the freedom of the town in 2018, and in 2021 a street near the football and cricket grounds was named after him.

And finally

He kept turning out for Accrington into his sixties. In 2009 he hit the winning runs in the last game of the season, as the club took its seventh Lancashire League title. Few cricketers get to sign off a playing life quite so neatly, with the bat in hand and the match won.
